lead: Three Node tools sit between your code and the disk. The fs module opens, reads, writes and deletes files. A stream carries the same bytes in small chunks, so a 1 GB file never has to sit in RAM. EventEmitter is the base pattern both rely on: an object emits a named event, and the functions listening for that name run. You meet all three in a log-writing server, a file-upload handler, a backup script, or anywhere a program moves data bigger than its memory.
prereq: You need callbacks, the event loop and microtasks from 6.1, plus arrow functions and promises from Unit 3.

sections.h3: The fs module: three flavours of the same call

blocks.text: Every file operation in Node lives in fs. The same job is offered in three shapes, and you pick one per call site.

items: Callback: fs.readFile(path, cb). The last argument is (err, data) and it runs later, after the disk answers.
Synchronous: the name ends in Sync, as in fs.readFileSync(path, 'utf8'). It returns the value directly, throws on failure, and stops the single thread until the disk is done.
Promises: require('fs/promises'), or require('fs').promises, gives the same functions returning promises, so const text = await fs.readFile(p, 'utf8') works.

head: Call
What it does
rows: whole file in, whole file out

blocks.text: readFile returns a Buffer unless you pass an encoding. Pass 'utf8' for text; keep the Buffer for images and video.

Join paths with path.join('data','logs','app.txt'). It picks the right separator for the operating system and collapses duplicate slashes. String concatenation with '/' breaks on Windows and happily produces data//logs.

sections.h3: Streams: move the file in chunks

blocks.text: A stream pushes data through in pieces instead of one big value. There are four kinds.

items: Duplex: both at once, such as a TCP socket.
Transform: a duplex that changes the bytes, such as gzip.

blocks.text: fs.createReadStream('big.mp4', {highWaterMark: 64 * 1024}) opens the file and emits a 'data' event per chunk. highWaterMark is the chunk size in bytes; the default is 64 KB = 65536 bytes.
read.pipe(write) wires the two together: each chunk is written to the destination, and the end of the source closes the destination. pipe returns the destination, so calls chain.

Backpressure makes this safe. When the write stream's internal buffer is full, write() returns false and pipe pauses the read stream until the writer emits 'drain'. A fast disk never floods a slow disk or a slow network; the reader simply waits.
pipe does not forward errors. Attach handlers yourself, or use stream.pipeline(read, write, cb), which destroys both sides and calls back once with the error.
require('events') gives the EventEmitter class. Streams, http servers and sockets are all EventEmitters underneath.

emitter.on('name', fn) registers a listener. emitter.emit('name', arg) calls every listener for that name at once, in registration order, passing arg. once('name', fn) runs the listener a single time and then removes it.
To build your own, extend the class. class Job extends EventEmitter {}, then const j = new Job(); j.on('done', n => console.log(n)); j.emit('done', 42); prints 42.

'error' is special. If you emit('error', err) and nobody is listening, Node throws err as an uncaught exception and the process exits. A stream that hits a disk failure emits 'error'; with no handler, your server dies.
'close' is not 'error'. It only means the file handle was released, and it can arrive after a clean end or after a failure. Never treat 'close' as proof of success.

figure.caption: One gigabyte moves through the program 64 KB at a time: the read stream fills a single buffer, pipe() hands that chunk on, and the reader waits whenever the writer is full. Peak memory stays near 64 KB instead of 1024 MB.

spec.aria: A 1 GB file is read in 64 KB chunks by a read stream and passed through a buffer to a write stream, so only one chunk sits in memory at a time before the copy is written to disk.

examples.question: A Node script copies a 1 GB video file to a backup disk. (a) How much RAM does fs.readFile need for this copy? (b) With createReadStream at highWaterMark: 64 * 1024, how many chunks are read and how much memory is live per step? (c) The backup disk fills up halfway. What happens if no 'error' listener is attached?
steps: 1 GB = 1024 MB, the binary unit that stat and file sizes use.
readFile must hold the whole file before the write starts, so memory ≈ 1024 MB.
Convert to kilobytes: 1024 MB × 1024 KB/MB = 1,048,576 KB.
Memory live per step ≈ 64 KB = 0.0625 MB. Check the ratio: 1024 MB ÷ 0.0625 MB = 16,384, the same number of chunks.
(c) The write stream emits 'error'. With zero listeners on that event, Node throws it as an uncaught exception and the process exits, leaving a half-written copy.
examples.answer: readFile needs about 1024 MB of RAM; the stream reads 16,384 chunks of 64 KB and keeps about 64 KB live at a time; a missing 'error' listener ends the process.
examples.check:
total_mb = 1024
chunk_kb = 64
total_kb = total_mb * 1024
chunks = total_kb // chunk_kb
print(total_mb)
print(total_kb)
print(chunks)

traps: readFile is asynchronous, so it does not block the event loop. Its problem is memory: the whole file is buffered. readFileSync is the one that blocks.
pipe() does not carry errors. If the destination disk fails, only the write stream's 'error' reports it. Listen on it, or use stream.pipeline.
'error' is not 'close'. 'close' only means the handle was released, and an unhandled 'error' throws and kills the process.
Missing encoding. readFile without 'utf8' returns a Buffer, so logging text shows hexadecimal bytes.
on() when you meant once(). A completion handler registered with on() fires again the next time that same emitter emits the event.

quiz.q: Name the three flavours of an fs call and one difference between them.
quiz.a: Callback (gets (err, data) later), Sync (returns the value, throws on error, blocks the thread), and promises (returns a promise, used with await).

quiz.q: What does highWaterMark control, and what is its default?
quiz.a: The chunk size in bytes for a stream. Default 64 KB = 65536 bytes.

quiz.q: Why does piping a 1 GB file use far less memory than readFile?
quiz.a: readFile buffers the entire file (about 1024 MB). A stream keeps roughly one chunk (about 64 KB) live and pauses while the writer's buffer is full, which is backpressure.

quiz.q: Why is the 'error' event special on an EventEmitter?
quiz.a: With no listener registered, emit('error', e) throws e as an uncaught exception, and the process exits instead of continuing silently.

quiz.q: A 512 MB file is read with highWaterMark set to 64 KB. How many chunks?
With const fs = require('fs/promises'), write the call that appends 'ok' to log.txt and the call that reads it back as text.
quiz.a: await fs.appendFile('log.txt', 'ok'); then const t = await fs.readFile('log.txt', 'utf8'); — the 'utf8' argument makes t a string, not a Buffer.

quiz.q: Four requests each run readFile on a 2 GB file at the same moment. Estimate the memory and say what you would change.
quiz.a: 4 × 2048 MB = 8192 MB ≈ 8 GB of RAM, which usually ends in an out-of-memory crash. Replace readFile with createReadStream and pipe the chunks to the response, so each request holds about 64 KB at a time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real code uses stream.pipeline and stream/promises instead of hand-wired pipe plus listeners, because they destroy both sides on failure. Node streams are async iterables, so for await (const chunk of readStream) works and reads like a loop. The WHATWG web streams standard now carries the same idea into browsers, Deno and Node, so a Transform written for one can often run in the others. Search for 'Node stream backpressure' and 'web streams TransformStream' next. Sending files over HTTP with streams belongs to 6.4.
